title: Microcosm: E. coli and the New Science of Life
author: Carl Zimmer
note: Eligible explanatory science narrative, not a laboratory curriculum. Disease is an application, not the dominant topic, so T11=0; the central subject is cellular mechanisms and discovery, so T12=0. No serious veto established: Nataro identifies specific mistakes and omissions, not failure of the central experimental account. Do not confuse this with George Gilder's different Microcosm. Mandatory Karpathy coverage; expert and reader praise is documented but not unanimous.
notes: JCI reviewer James Nataro praises the account but identifies incorrect flagellar illustrations, peptide charge and thin coverage of commensal strains; these limit E without invalidating the whole narrative.
Connects molecular machinery, experimental methods, evolution and biotechnology; industrial institutions receive less attention.
Useful models of feedback, resource allocation and experimental inference; transfer to engineering is an interpretation, not an experimentally demonstrated equivalence.
Explains gene regulation, bacterial exchange and adaptation through experiments and cellular processes.

D=8/10, moderate confidence: contents, Nataro's review, Science News and Karpathy's reading report. Gene regulation, motility, cooperation and engineering add distinct learning. Some readers report a slow pace and uneven transitions; no full-text density audit.
Experimental history and basic mechanisms remain durable; contemporary biotechnology examples reflect 2008 knowledge.
Strong for biological machinery and scientific method; less direct than industrial or computing history.
Established science reporter; substantive assessment by an E. coli specialist supports authority while exposing limitations.
A single model organism gives the narrative coherence; the final applications broaden its scope.
Generally precise and accessible explanation, with occasional literary flourishes.

title: Wetware: A Computer in Every Living Cell
author: Dennis Bray
note: Eligible sustained explanation of cellular information processing; no specialist curriculum or procedural training. Molecular computation is central, so T11=T12=0. Distinguish documented biochemical signaling from broader analogies with cognition. No high-confidence foundational veto established. Later research still uses the wetware framework; some robotics comparisons are dated. Karpathy marked this to-read, which is provenance, not praise.
notes: Specialist author's molecular account is supported by subsequent cellular-computation research. Generalizations about intelligence and machines are less secure than the biochemical examples.
Integrates proteins, signaling, cellular behavior, networks and computation, but connects little to industrial institutions.
Useful analogies for distributed sensing, adaptation and control, provided biological and engineered systems are not treated as identical.
Explains switches, chemical signaling and network responses at molecular scale.

D=7.5/10, moderate confidence from contents and contrasting reading reports. Protein switches, signaling and cellular wiring add distinct mechanisms. Later robotics and neural-network discussions are reported as less focused; added cases are not automatically counted as padding.
Cellular mechanisms have lasting value; 2009 views of robotics and artificial intelligence require historical context.
Direct connection to computation, modeling, feedback and complex mechanisms.
Cambridge cell biologist and computational-biology prize recipient, with specialist attention in Artificial Life and later scientific literature.
Concrete cellular examples aid comprehension; movement between levels can make the structure uneven.
Accessible prose, but the computation metaphor can suggest more equivalence than the evidence warrants.

title: Journey to the Ants: A Story of Scientific Exploration
author: Bert Hölldobler; Edward O. Wilson
note: Eligible general-reader natural history and scientific memoir, distinct from the technical reference The Ants. The final practical section does not make the main work a technical curriculum. Ecology and natural history predominate, so T11=-10; social organization is biological, not centrally human power or military doctrine, so T12=0. No serious veto established. Scientific authority and reader reception are strong; publisher praise for The Ants must not be transferred to this separate book.
notes: First-hand scientific observation by leading ant researchers. Evolutionary interpretation needs distinction from directly observed colony behavior.
Integrates individual behavior, colony organization, communication and environmental relations; broader human technological layers are limited.
Mechanisms of decentralized coordination, division of labor and resource management offer transferable models, with limits on human analogies.
Explains chemical communication, cooperation, parasitism and colony-level organization through concrete cases.

D=8/10, moderate confidence from contents, Publishers Weekly and Karpathy's detailed reading report. Chemical signaling, leafcutter cultivation and social parasites add different mechanisms. Memoir adds discovery context; no evidence here for a precise removable-page estimate.
Observational natural history and colony mechanisms retain value across technological cycles.
Relevant to distributed systems and scientific organization by analogy; biological natural history is outside the central preferred domains.
Authors are established specialist researchers. Their earlier reference won a Pulitzer; that award belongs to the earlier work, not this book.
Personal exploration and vivid organism-level cases make the narrative approachable.
Clear explanatory language; anthropomorphic labels should not be mistaken for literal human institutions.

title: Profiles of the Future: An Inquiry into the Limits of the Possible
author: Arthur C. Clarke
note: Nonfiction speculative essays, despite the fiction-imprint categorization on one publisher page. Eligible discussion of physical possibilities and forecasting errors. No veto merely because forecasts failed: speculation is explicit and revised editions acknowledge errors. Do not use this as current technology guidance. Review reception is mixed, so inclusion is through mandatory Karpathy coverage, not a claim of consensus praise. No single central historical period; H13=0. Original 1962 publication governs P14.
notes: Physical constraints discipline some forecasts, but feasibility and adoption predictions are uneven. Explicit speculation and acknowledged forecasting failure distinguish this from concealed uncertainty.
Relates scientific possibilities to transport, communications and material supply; economic and institutional constraints receive weaker treatment.
Forecasting failure modes and the distinction between impossibility and practical difficulty remain useful.
Explains selected technological constraints, but many future scenarios are sketches rather than developed causal analyses.

D=6.5/10, moderate confidence from Kirkus and named reader reports including Karpathy. Opening forecasting examples are useful; later scenarios vary in learning yield and some readers report diminishing returns. This is a density judgment, separate from their factual obsolescence.
Forecasting humility is durable; much specific technological speculation has aged poorly.
Directly addresses technological limits, engineering and future capabilities.
Scientifically trained and historically influential technology writer, not a comprehensive authority on every discussed field.
Lively essay structure is accessible but less cumulative than a sustained argument.
Memorable formulations, sometimes more sweeping than the supporting analysis.
